hints: Compare the shapes of the two substrates. Which one is a simple unbranched chain and which one is highly branched with extra branch-point bonds?
Remember which bonds make the straight chains and which make the branches. Enzyme X can only cut alpha-1,4 bonds, so ask yourself what is left uncut in each molecule.
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of amylose and glycogen**

Both are polymers of alpha-glucose joined mainly by alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds.

Amylose is unbranched, so it has only alpha-1,4 bonds. Glycogen is highly branched, so it has many alpha-1,4 bonds plus alpha-1,6 bonds at every branch point.

**Apply what enzyme X can do**

Enzyme X only breaks $\alpha$-1,4 bonds. It cannot break $\alpha$-1,6 branch-point bonds.

So for complete hydrolysis, every single bond must be broken, and enzyme X alone cannot do that where 1,6 bonds exist.

**Decide the level of hydrolysis**

For amylose: all bonds are 1,4, so enzyme X can break almost all of them. That is most hydrolysis, ++.

For glycogen: enzyme X breaks the 1,4 sections but leaves the 1,6 branch points intact. That is only some hydrolysis, +.

options.A: Correct. Glycogen gets + (some hydrolysis, 1,6 branches remain) and amylose gets ++ (most hydrolysis, all bonds are 1,4).
options.B: Reversed. Glycogen cannot be hydrolysed more completely than amylose because its 1,6 branches resist enzyme X.
options.C: Wrong for amylose. Amylose has no 1,6 bonds, so enzyme X gives most hydrolysis, not no hydrolysis.
options.D: Wrong for glycogen. Glycogen has many 1,4 bonds that enzyme X can break, so some hydrolysis occurs, not zero.
